text:
Keep the Join: Why Primary Schools Should Still Teach Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone declares joined-up handwriting obsolete. The argument usually goes like this: children will spend their adult lives typing, tapping and dictating, so the hours spent on loops and lead-in strokes would be better given to coding, keyboard skills or more reading. Finland dropped the requirement for cursive in 2016 in favour of typing. In the United States, the Common Core standards adopted around 2010 left cursive out altogether, and many schools quietly stopped teaching it.

The argument sounds modern and sensible. I think it is wrong. Primary schools should go on teaching joined-up handwriting. They should teach it as a practical tool for thinking and writing at speed, and nostalgia has nothing to do with it. The case rests on how children learn to read and spell, on what fluent handwriting frees up in a young writer's mind, on fairness in examinations, and on the plain fact that pens have not gone away.

What handwriting does for the brain

The strongest reason to keep teaching handwriting of any kind is that forming letters by hand seems to help children learn them. In a much-cited study, the psychologist Karin James at Indiana University scanned the brains of young children who had practised letters in different ways. Children who had written letters by hand showed more activity in brain regions linked with reading than children who had typed or traced them. Researchers in Norway, Audrey van der Meer and Ruud van der Weel, have reported similar results using EEG with older children and young adults: handwriting produced wider patterns of connectivity in the brain than typing did.

None of this proves that cursive in particular is magic, and honest advocates should say so. Much of the research compares handwriting with typing, not joined script with print. But the findings matter for the cursive debate all the same, because joined-up writing is where handwriting becomes fluent. A child who prints each letter as a separate act is still, in effect, drawing. A child who joins is writing words as units of movement. The hand learns that "-ing" and "th" and "ough" are shapes that belong together, and that physical memory supports spelling. Teachers in English primary schools often describe this: children who join confidently tend to spell common letter strings more reliably, because the word lives in the hand as well as the eye.

The national curriculum in England already reflects this view. It expects children in Key Stage 2 to use the diagonal and horizontal strokes needed to join letters and to understand which letters are best left unjoined. That expectation was not an accident of tradition. It came from a long-standing belief among literacy specialists that handwriting, spelling and composition develop together.

Fluency frees the mind for thinking

Writing is hard work for a seven-year-old. In a single sentence they have to hold an idea in mind, find the words, sort out grammar and punctuation, recall spellings and physically form the letters. Psychologists talk about working memory as a small desk with limited space. If letter formation is slow and effortful, it takes up room on that desk that should be used for the actual ideas.

This is the practical case for joined-up writing. Once it is learned, it is usually faster than print, because the pen leaves the paper less often. More important, it becomes automatic. A child who no longer has to think about how to make a "k" can think about whether the sentence makes sense. Studies of children's writing have repeatedly found that handwriting fluency predicts the quality and length of what children compose, not just its neatness. The child who writes slowly writes less, revises less, and often gives up sooner.

Critics reply that keyboards offer the same automaticity. In principle they could, but in practice most primary-aged children are not fast touch-typists, and teaching touch-typing well takes as much time as teaching joined handwriting. More to the point, children still write by hand for most of their school day: in exercise books, on mini whiteboards, on worksheets, on sticky notes during a science experiment. Until schools are prepared to put a keyboard in front of every child in every lesson, handwriting remains the main way young children get their thoughts down. It makes sense to give them the fastest and most fluent version of it.

Speed and fairness in examinations

The second practical argument concerns the examination hall. In the UK, GCSEs and A levels are still overwhelmingly handwritten. A sixteen-year-old sitting a two-hour English Literature paper is expected to produce several pages of extended argument under time pressure. Students who never learned to join often write slowly and tire quickly, and their hands cramp. Many end up with access arrangements, such as extra time or a word processor, that they might not have needed had they been given a fluent script at age eight.

There is a fairness point here. Children from homes where parents write letters, keep diaries or model handwriting may pick up a fluent hand anyway. Children without those advantages depend on school. If primary schools stop teaching joined-up writing, the skill does not vanish. It becomes something that better-off families pass on privately, and another small gap opens up. Universal teaching of a basic skill is one of the ways state education levels the ground, and handwriting is one of those skills.

Exam boards may move further towards on-screen assessment in time. Some are trialling it. But a child who starts primary school this year will sit most of their important exams by hand, and the system should prepare them for the world as it is.

Pens have not gone away

The claim that handwriting is obsolete also overstates how little adults write. Doctors, nurses and care workers still annotate charts. Teachers mark by hand. Engineers sketch and label on site. Most of us still sign documents, fill in forms, write birthday cards, leave notes for a neighbour, and jot down a phone number when no device is to hand. Note-taking by hand has also had something of a revival, helped by research such as Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer's 2014 study, which found that students who took lecture notes by hand tended to understand the material better than those who typed, apparently because the slower pace forced them to summarise rather than transcribe.

Then there is reading. A generation that cannot write joined-up script often struggles to read it. Grandparents' letters, old family recipes, archive documents, historical records and a good deal of everyday handwriting from other people are written in some form of joined hand. This is part of why several American states, including California in 2023, have passed laws to bring cursive back into elementary schools after a decade of decline. Legislators heard from teachers, archivists and parents who had found that young people could not read their own family history.

Answering the objections

The strongest objection is about time. The primary timetable is crowded, and every hour spent on handwriting is an hour not spent on something else. This is a fair concern, but it misjudges how much time is involved. Good handwriting teaching does not need long daily sessions of copying. Short, frequent practice, often ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week, is what works. Much of the gain comes from applying the joined style in ordinary writing across the curriculum, which costs nothing extra. Set against the benefits to spelling, composition and exam performance, it is a modest investment.

A second objection is that some children, especially those with dyspraxia or other motor difficulties, find joined writing very hard. That is true, and schools should be flexible. Some children will be better served by a clear print script or by early access to a keyboard, and no child should be held back because their loops are untidy. But the right response to a minority who struggle is to adapt for them. It is not to remove a useful skill from everyone else. In fact, many occupational therapists argue that a continuous joined style can help some children with motor difficulties, because it reduces the number of times the pen has to be lifted and repositioned.

A third objection is that the old obsession with neatness did real harm. Children were scolded for messy loops, and handwriting was treated as a measure of character. That history is worth remembering, but it argues for teaching handwriting better, not abandoning it. The goal is a legible, comfortable, fast hand. It does not have to be a copperplate showpiece. Modern handwriting schemes in England reflect this, focusing on simple joins and practical speed rather than ornament.

A skill worth keeping

Schools are always under pressure to drop the old and add the new, and much of that pressure is healthy. But some skills last because they do real work. Joined-up handwriting helps children learn letters and spellings, frees their minds to compose, prepares them for handwritten exams, and lets them read and write the handwritten documents they will still meet as adults. It is cheap to teach, takes little time when done well, and it is fairest when the state guarantees it for every child rather than leaving it to families.

Keyboards and handwriting are not rivals. Children should learn both, at different stages and for different purposes. The mistake would be to assume that because adults type more than they used to, children no longer need to learn to write fluently by hand. Primary schools should keep teaching the join.
